teaser.text: Vulcan Materials Company sells the heavy, ordinary-looking materials that make construction possible: stone, sand, gravel, asphalt mix and ready-mixed concrete. Its business is local and physical, so a dollar enters when a specified load or completed job is sold and leaves through extraction, processing, delivery, labor, equipment and the costs of keeping the network ready.

stock.opening: Vulcan's weighted price reaches $271.06 by October 2029. It hinges on whether infrastructure and large projects sustain volumes while energy pressure eases.
stock.closing: The full Vulcan memo also answers how Vulcan’s business works, who its rivals are, how management allocates capital, and what risks shape the cases.

paragraphs.text: The forecast points to modest weighted returns, but the possible outcomes are widely dispersed. At October 2027, the weighted price is $246.54, a 3% loss with dividends. At October 2028, it is $255.36, a 1% gain. At October 2029, it reaches $271.06, an 8% gain.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Vulcan, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The base forecast assumes gradual improvement in shipments and pricing. Normal operating profit is $1,800 million in October 2027 and rises to $2,000 million by October 2029. Infrastructure and large projects must sustain volumes while energy pressure eases. Project delays and rising unit costs strengthen the bear case. The next scheduled release is October 29, 2026.

The bull case requires infrastructure and large private projects to sustain volumes while weather and energy costs improve. Pricing then flows more fully into unit profit, and stronger cash generation supports debt reduction and repurchases. The price reaches $306.23 by October 2027 and $431.09 by October 2029. The probability is 20% because the Q2 cost experience, uncertain acquisition returns, and finite buyback authorization make sustained expansion less dependable.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Vulcan really make?

paragraphs.text: Stock compensation is another claim on the cash economics because employees receive an ownership interest. Vulcan recorded $63.1 million of stock pay in 2025; deducting it produces an analytical “real” free-cash-flow figure. Acquisitions remain outside Vulcan’s free-cash-flow definition, so a cash-generating company can still borrow heavily when it buys another quarry.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Vulcan today?

paragraphs.text: The trailing P/E uses the last twelve months of earnings, while the forward P/E uses the next twelve months. The lower forward multiple therefore assumes improvement. It is not simply a cheaper price for the same profits. EBITDA is broader operating profit before interest, tax, and noncash asset charges, but it is not cash available to shareholders. Vulcan spent $702.9 million replacing or improving property, plant, and equipment in 2025, so quarry maintenance absorbs part of what EBITDA appears to produce. Using October 20, 2026 enterprise value and trailing adjusted EBITDA through June 2026 gives an illustrative EV/EBITDA multiple of about 15.9x.

blocks.heading: Does Vulcan's cash flow cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Capital expenditure, or capex, is spending on plants, machinery and quarry improvements. Vulcan spent $677.7 million on capex in 2025. After that spending, free cash flow was $1,135.3 million, making it a better starting point for debt repayment or shareholder returns than cash gross profit.

Stock compensation is another claim on the cash economics because employees receive an ownership interest. Vulcan recorded $63.1 million of stock pay in 2025; deducting it produces an analytical “real” free-cash-flow figure. Acquisitions remain outside Vulcan’s free-cash-flow definition, so a cash-generating company can still borrow heavily when it buys another quarry.

paragraphs.text: Base dividends rise from $2.20 per share to $2.36 and then $2.52. This follows five consecutive annual increases and the latest $0.52 quarterly declaration. The bear case holds at $2.08 in each period, while the bull case reaches $2.74 as stronger cash generation supports faster increases. Capital spending of $750–$800 million makes the bull path less certain.

The forecast would move toward the bear case if 2027 project starts and public awards are delayed, or if energy and other unit costs again outpace realized prices. A weaker earnings path in 2028–2029 would also compress the multiple.

earnings.title: Vulcan earnings date and guidance
earnings.meta_description: Vulcan expects results on October 29, 2026, with guidance for shipment growth, price improvement and capital spending.
earnings.opening: Vulcan's next results are scheduled for October 29, 2026. The key thing to watch is whether price improvement survives energy and other production costs.
earnings.closing: The full memo also answers how Vulcan's business works, who its rivals are, how Vulcan's management is paid and overseen, and what risks Vulcan faces.

paragraphs.text: Management guides to 1%–3% shipment growth and 4%–6% freight-adjusted price improvement in 2026.

Management plans $750–$800 million of 2026 capital spending for maintenance and growth. Maintenance keeps existing equipment productive. Growth spending adds capacity or improves access to customers. Replacing a worn crusher protects current output, while adding a rail yard can help a quarry reach another market.

blocks.heading: Has Vulcan kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Management’s promises have produced a mixed record. The 2025 adjusted EBITDA forecast came in below its stated range, but aggregates cash gross profit per ton improved from 2024 to 2025. The June 2026 ambition of US$20 per ton remains a promise rather than an achieved result.

blocks.heading: What has Vulcan's last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: The proper comparison is June with June because construction is seasonal. Revenue rose from $2,102.4 million in the second quarter of 2025 to $2,155.8 million in the second quarter of 2026. Aggregate shipments increased about 1%, supported by public construction and large projects, while rain disrupted Texas and parts of the Southeast.

Repair and insurance timing also affected the comparisons. Work pushed out by weather can make a later quarter look better, but the repairs still belong to the economics. The table provides the fuller eight-quarter sequence needed to distinguish an isolated quarter from a trend.
